request.query: Which passages state the same fact as either of these two statements? (1) `From` reaches the compiled pattern as a regular expression, so the other regexp metacharacters keep their meaning: `/a.b` also matches `/aXb`, and `/faq?` also matches `/fa`. (2) With neither, the middleware rewrites nothing. A rule's `From` is path text: `*` matches a run of any bytes but a newline, and every other byte stands for itself, so `/preis-1.000-euro` rewrites that path and not `/preis-1X000-euro`.
request.instructions: A passage answers only if it itself states the fact that the two statements disagree about: a value, version, limit, name, list or rule for the same thing. A passage that only mentions the topic does not answer.

documents.title: docs/whats_new.md > 📋 Migration guide > 🧬 Middlewares > Rewrite
docs/guide/error-handling.md > Custom Error Handler
documents.text: A sub-app mounted with `app.Use` can set its own `ErrorHandler`. It answers every error raised under the mount path, including the **404** for a path that matches none of the sub-app's routes. An app mounted inside it without a handler of its own uses it too, and any other request falls back to the parent's handler. This needs a literal mount path, taken from the top-level app down: the lookup compares the request path with the mount path as text, so under a parameter, as in `app.Use("/t/:tenant", tenantApp)`, the sub-app's routes still match and run but its handler is not found, and neither is the handler of an app mounted inside it. The handler of the nearest enclosing mount with a literal path answers instead, or the top-level app's handler when there is none. A sub-app mounted through [`Domain`](../api/app.md#domain) matches a parameterized mount path as a pattern and keeps its own handler.

documents.title: docs/middleware/expvar.md > ExpVar > Examples
documents.text:
## Examples

Import the middleware package:

```go
import (
    "expvar"
    "fmt"

    "github.com/gofiber/fiber/v3"
    expvarmw "github.com/gofiber/fiber/v3/middleware/expvar"
)
```

Once your Fiber app is initialized, use the middleware as shown:

```go
var count = expvar.NewInt("count")

app.Use(expvarmw.New())
app.Get("/", func(c fiber.Ctx) error {
    count.Add(1)

    return c.SendString(fmt.Sprintf("hello expvar count %d", count.Value()))
})
```

Visit `/debug/vars` to see all variables, and append `?r=<regexp>` to keep only the variables whose names match the regular expression; an invalid expression is answered with `400 Bad Request`. Any path beneath `/debug/vars/` is redirected to `/debug/vars` with `303 See Other`, and every other path continues down the handler chain.

```bash
curl 127.0.0.1:3000
hello expvar count 1

curl 127.0.0.1:3000/debug/vars
{
    "cmdline": ["xxx"],
    "count": 1,
    "expvarHandlerCalls": 33,
    "expvarRegexpErrors": 0,
    "memstats": {...}
}

curl 127.0.0.1:3000/debug/vars?r=c
{
    "cmdline": ["xxx"],
    "count": 1
}
```

documents.title: docs/middleware/rewrite.md > Rewrite > Rule order
documents.text:
## Rule order

Rules are tried in the order you write them and the first one whose `From`
matches answers, exactly as [routes](../guide/routing.md) are matched. Nothing
reorders a `RuleList`. Put the specific rules before the catch-alls:

```go
RuleList: []rewrite.Rule{
    {From: "/api/users", To: "/v2/users"},  // checked first
    {From: "/api/*", To: "/v2/$1"},         // takes everything else
}
```

Written the other way round, `/api/*` answers `/api/users` too and the second
rule never fires.

:::note
The deprecated `Rules` map has no order of its own, so Fiber sorts it: most path
text before the first `*` wins, then most path text overall, then fewest
asterisks, then the key itself. That is a rough reading of "most specific", not
an exact one, so a long wildcard rule can still outrank a shorter exact one.
`RuleList` is the exact control.
:::

documents.title: docs/middleware/redirect.md > Redirect > Rule order
documents.text:
## Rule order

Rules are tried in the order you write them and the first one whose `From`
matches answers, exactly as [routes](../guide/routing.md) are matched. Nothing
reorders a `RuleList`. Put the specific rules before the catch-alls:

```go
RuleList: []redirect.Rule{
    {From: "/api/users", To: "/v2/users"},  // checked first
    {From: "/api/*", To: "/v2/$1"},         // takes everything else
}
```

Written the other way round, `/api/*` answers `/api/users` too and the second
rule never fires. For lists of 100 rules or fewer, Fiber logs a warning at startup naming any rule
an earlier one shadows outright, so a dead rule tells you rather than going
quiet.

The deprecated `Rules` map has no order of its own, so Fiber sorts it: most path
text pinned before the first `*` or other regular-expression character wins,
then most path text overall, then fewest asterisks, then the key itself. That
covers rules written with path text and `*`. Rules relying on
regular-expression syntax beyond `*` may order differently. Use `RuleList`,
where the order is yours.

documents.title: docs/guide/routing.md > Parameters > Constraints
documents.text:
### Constraints

Route constraints execute when a match has occurred to the incoming URL and the URL path is tokenized into route values by parameters. The feature was introduced in `v2.37.0` and inspired by [.NET Core](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/routing?view=aspnetcore-6.0#route-constraints).

:::caution
Constraints are matching rules, not input validation: if a value fails a constraint, the route simply does not match and Fiber returns **404 Not Found**.
:::

| Constraint        | Example                          | Example matches                                                                             |
| ----------------- | -------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| int               | `:id<int>`                       | 123456789, -123456789                                                                       |
| bool              | `:active<bool>`                  | true, false (and the other values `strconv.ParseBool` reads, such as 1 and 0)               |
| guid              | `:id<guid>`                      | CD2C1638-1638-72D5-1638-DEADBEEF1638                                                        |
| float             | `:weight<float>`                 | 1.234, -1001.01e8, 3.14                                                                     |
| minLen(value)     | `:username<minLen(4)>`           | Test (must be at least 4 bytes)                                                             |
| maxLen(value)     | `:filename<maxLen(8)>`           | MyFile (must be no more than 8 bytes)                                                       |
| len(length)       | `:filename<len(12)>`             | somefile.txt (exactly 12 bytes)                                                             |
| betweenLen(min,max) | `:name<betweenLen(3,8)>`       | MyFile (must be at least 3 and no more than 8 bytes)                                        |
| min(value)        | `:age<min(18)>`                  | 19 (Integer value must be at least 18)                                                      |
| max(value)        | `:age<max(120)>`                 | 91 (Integer value must be no more than 120)                                                 |
| range(min,max)    | `:age<range(18,120)>`            | 91 (Integer value must be at least 18 but no more than 120)                                 |
| alpha             | `:name<alpha>`                   | Rick (String must consist of one or more letters: a-z in either case, and other Unicode letters when the path reaches the router as UTF-8, which a percent-encoded path does only with [`UnescapePath`](../api/fiber.md#unescapepath) enabled) |
| datetime          | `:dob<datetime(2006\\-01\\-02)>` | 2005-11-01                                                                                  |
| regex(expression) | `:date<regex(\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2})>` | 2022-08-27 (Must match regular expression)                                                  |

documents.title: README.md > Zero Allocation
documents.text:
## Zero Allocation

Fiber is optimized for **high-performance**, meaning values returned from **fiber.Ctx** are **not** immutable by default and **will** be reused across requests. As a rule of thumb, you **must** only use context values within the handler and **must not** keep any references. Once you return from the handler, any values obtained from the context will be reused in future requests. Visit our [documentation](https://docs.gofiber.io/#zero-allocation) to learn more.

documents.title: docs/api/app.md > Routing > Domain
documents.text:
Domain routing has **zero performance impact** on routes that don't use it — the hostname check is applied as a handler wrapper, not a change to the core router.

:::note
Because domain filtering is applied at handler-execution time (not during route matching), Fiber's `405 Method Not Allowed` logic may advertise methods from domain-scoped routes even when the requesting host does not match the domain pattern. This is a known trade-off of the handler-wrapping approach — it avoids core router changes while keeping non-domain routes unaffected.
:::

:::note
When mounting sub-applications via `Domain(...).Use(*fiber.App)`, routes are cloned from the sub-app at mount time. This means the same sub-app can safely be mounted on multiple domains without double-wrapping, but routes registered on the sub-app **after** mounting will not inherit domain filtering. Register all sub-app routes before mounting.

Apps that the sub-app has mounted itself are cloned along with it, so nested routes are domain-filtered as well. The same "register before mounting" rule applies to them.

A domain-mounted sub-app's `ErrorHandler` and `Views` are host-scoped like its routes: they apply to requests whose hostname matches the pattern, and requests on other hosts fall back to the parent's. Two sub-apps mounted at the same path on different domains therefore keep their own configuration. A sub-app that sets none of its own inherits them from the app it is mounted inside, as with a plain mount; a separately mounted app that merely covers the same paths and hosts is not inherited from.
:::

documents.title: docs/api/app.md > Routing > Mounting
documents.text:
A sub-app's own [`ErrorHandler`](#errorhandler), `Views` and `ViewsLayout` still apply to the requests under its mount path, but only when the whole mount path, from the top-level app down, is literal. Under a parameter, as in `app.Use("/t/:tenant", tenantApp)`, the routes match and run while the nearest enclosing mount with a literal path, or the top-level app, supplies the error handler and the view engine. A [`Domain`](#domain) mount matches a parameterized path as a pattern, so its sub-app keeps its own. The [`RegexHandler`](./fiber.md#regexhandler) of a sub-app mounted on the top-level app compiles the `regex()` constraints in the full path of every route below it, the mount prefix included, so an app mounted deeper does not use its own.
:::

documents.title: docs/guide/routing.md > Parameters > Constraints
documents.text:
The length constraints (`minLen`, `maxLen`, `len` and `betweenLen`) count bytes, not characters, of the value the router matched: a non-ASCII character counts as its UTF-8 bytes, or as its longer `%XX` form while the path keeps it percent-encoded, which is the default (see [`UnescapePath`](../api/fiber.md#unescapepath)).

Constraint names and arguments are always taken from the pattern as written, even with the default case-insensitive routing: `:code<regex([A-Z]{2})>` keeps matching uppercase codes only, a `datetime` layout keeps its `T` and `Z`, and a custom constraint registered under a mixed-case name is found. A built-in name matches in any letter case (`minLen(4)` and `MinLen(4)` are the same constraint), while a custom constraint name must match exactly.

:::note
A constraint with a missing or malformed argument (`:id<min>` or `:id<min(abc)>`) never matches, so the route answers **404** for every request. A name that is neither built in nor a registered [custom constraint](#custom-constraint) is ignored and leaves the parameter unconstrained, so a misspelled constraint does not reject anything. Only `regex(...)` expressions are checked when the route is registered: an invalid one panics.
:::

documents.title: docs/middleware/static.md > Static > Examples > SPA (Single Page Application)
documents.text:
A root that is a single file looks nothing up by the path, so it serves its file for every other path the route matches, whatever its spelling, and no spelling of a path can select another file. An empty segment further in is an ordinary part of a name there, as in `/web/https://example.com`.
:::

:::tip
A client that puts a doubled slash in front of a path, such as a base URL that ends in `/` joined to a path that starts with `/`, gets `404 Not Found` from a root mount. To keep serving it, collapse the slash with the [Rewrite](./rewrite.md) middleware before any middleware that matches a path prefix runs. The middleware registered after it, one guarding `/private` included, then sees `/private/secret.txt`:

```go
app.Use(rewrite.New(rewrite.Config{
    RuleList: []rewrite.Rule{{From: "//*", To: "/$1"}},
}))
```

:::

:::caution
The file server opens the name the router matched, so it is only as strict as the filesystem underneath. On Windows a path component loses its trailing dots and spaces when it is opened, so `/static/private./secret.txt` would reach `private/secret.txt` without passing middleware mounted on `/static/private`; the file server answers such a segment with `404 Not Found` on Windows, whatever the root: an `fs.FS` may be OS-backed (`os.DirFS`) and cannot be told apart from a virtual one such as `embed.FS`, so an embedded name ending in a dot or a space is not served on Windows either. Case is a different matter: on a case-insensitive filesystem (Windows, and macOS by default) `/static/PRIVATE/secret.txt` opens `private/secret.txt`, and with [`CaseSensitive`](../api/fiber.md#config) enabled the router keeps the two apart, so middleware mounted on `/static/private` does not run. Leave `CaseSensitive` off (the default) for a static root with guarded directories, or serve it from a case-sensitive filesystem.
:::

documents.title: docs/middleware/basicauth.md > BasicAuth > Examples > Password hashes
documents.text:
### Password hashes

Passwords must be supplied in pre-hashed form. The middleware detects the
hashing algorithm from a prefix:

- `"{SHA512}"` or `"{SHA256}"` followed by a base64-encoded digest
- standard bcrypt strings beginning with `$2`

If no prefix is present, the value is interpreted as a SHA-256 digest encoded in
hex or base64. Plaintext passwords are rejected.

The middleware decodes the credentials as UTF-8 and normalizes them to Unicode
NFC before it compares them, so hash a password that contains non-ASCII
characters in its NFC form. Credentials that are not valid UTF-8, or that
contain control characters, are answered with `400 Bad Request`.

The decoded digest must be exactly the size of the named algorithm — 32 bytes
for SHA-256, 64 bytes for SHA-512. A digest of any other length could never
match a password, so it is rejected at startup: `New()` panics with
`ErrInvalidSHA256PasswordLength` or `ErrInvalidSHA512PasswordLength` rather than
starting with an account that can never authenticate. The most common cause is
a truncated copy/paste, or a SHA-256 digest stored under the `{SHA512}` prefix.

Every attempt runs one check per configured hash tier, meaning each algorithm
and each bcrypt cost in `Users`, whether the user exists or not, so response
time reveals neither. A setup with a single tier pays for one check. A mixed
one, for example while migrating from SHA-256 to bcrypt or to a higher bcrypt
cost, pays for one check per tier on every attempt.
